Changing only the step where such a failure starts repairs it more often than changing a similar earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models. Our code is available at https://github.com/rmakarovv/fast-at-the-frontier.
item.dc:creator: Roman Makarov, Zhe Xu, Jian Kang

item.title: When Should Decision Models Compare Candidates?
item.description: Language-model agents frequently select among candidate actions, such as tools and web elements. Should decision models score candidates independently or allow their scores to depend on other candidates? We investigate this question by comparing three approaches: Pointwise scoring, Setwise scoring, and Candidate Attention. Across five agent-decision benchmarks, Pointwise scoring remains competitive, while Setwise scoring performs better on some tool-selection and binary-decision tasks. Candidate Attention does not consistently improve upon Pointwise scoring, despite allowing cross-candidate interaction. Using two controlled synthetic tasks, we further examine whether models learn to use candidate-set information. With targeted relational training, Setwise models learn candidate dependencies and generalize to shifted inputs, while Candidate Attention shows weaker transfer. Our results show that access to other candidates does not guarantee effective comparison, and that its benefits depend on both task requirements and training.
item.dc:creator: Fangzhi Li, Quan Shi, Wenting Yang, Yueqiao Chen, Jiayu Chang, Shuting Zhao, Zhaowei Xu, Yizhao Chen, Guanchu Wu, Han Xu

item.title: Offline-First Quantized AI: Design and Evaluation of an On-Device Maternal-Health Assistant for Low-Connectivity Environments
item.description: Offline language models could extend access to maternal-health information where internet connectivity is unreliable, but deployment requires both clinically appropriate responses and feasible local execution. This study presents an offline Android assistant integrating ready-made quantized language models, a clinically validated local knowledge package, conversational context, and model-initiated local retrieval. Gemma 4 E2B and Qwen3.5 0.8B were compared across 45 conversations and 312 turns per configuration, including a dedicated offline agentic benchmark. Gemma achieved higher response-quality, context-retention, and safety scores; Qwen offered faster generation and lower memory use. Clinician assessment of 150 Gemma responses across nine clinical domains yielded a mean quality score of 3.80/4, with 147 responses meeting the acceptance criterion. A paired RAG-on/off experiment evaluated 74 questions: retrieval improved 11 responses, left 56 neutral, produced four adverse response changes, and left three pairs unassessable. RAG-on had descriptively higher mean usefulness, safety, correctness, and actionability in the conditional 70-pair subset excluding the four flagged pairs from both conditions. Physical-device testing demonstrated offline responses on a 6 GB Android handset, with a 14.3 s median latency, alongside successful reconnection synchronization in the integrated application. Together, the findings document clinical response quality and practical performance of the integrated offline maternal-health assistant.
item.dc:creator: Okenla AbdulQahhar Abimbola, Maurice Abraham John, Adepoju Jeremiah Moyondafoluwa, Omolaiye Samuel, Oko-Oba Sandra Chioma, Owoo Oluwamayowa Emmanuel, Thanni Adewuyi, Lily Aimas-Love, Benson Eniola, Abdulquddus Ajibade, Sylvia Essessien, Anyanwu Princess Emmanuella, Adereni Abiodun

item.title: NoLBERT-Calls: Reading Earnings Calls Without Hindsight
item.description: Language models are now a standard tool for measuring what managers say on earnings calls, but the encoders behind these measures were usually pretrained on text from the same years a backtest covers. Holding out a test period does not remove that hindsight, because it sits in the features. We adapt NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, to earnings calls without letting it read anything dated after 31 December 2023. The calls supply the training signal themselves: every analyst question is followed by management's answer, and the model learns to pick that answer out from the other answers of the same call. We test on every US call from January 2025 to October 2026 (20,323 calls, 254,575 questions) and make every modeling choice on calls from 2024. The adapted model, NoLBERT-Calls-2023, ranks the true answer first for 78.0% of questions (95% interval 77.8-78.2; chance 8.0%), against 26.3% before adaptation. It is 1.0 point ahead of a call-adapted ChronoBERT, 3.4 points ahead of a call-adapted FinBERT, and 18.7 and 19.8 points ahead of the best off-the-shelf retriever and BM25. A year-by-year test over 2013-2026 finds no look-ahead premium: relative to a model adapted only through 2012, the released model does no better on the years it was trained on than on years it never saw. The price of the cutoff is compute: under one shared 150-minute recipe NoLBERT adapts least well of four encoders, and its lead comes from a longer, staged adaptation of about 13 GPU-hours.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Foley, Jonathan Hartadi, Shivesh Prakash, Hino Wirachapong Suwanphibun, Swapnil Vatsal

item.title: Leakage-aware calibrated decision-level fusion for mental-health text classification
item.description: Decision-level fusion benefits from complementary errors, calibrated probabilities, and leakage-aware evaluation. We evaluated a heterogeneous transformer fusion framework on 262,276 proxy-labeled Reddit records covering anxiety, depression, schizophrenia, and suicidal ideation. In a stratified random split, MinHash-LSH identified 29.1% of test records as lexical near-duplicates of training data. Augmentation-lineage auditing found 50.2% lineage overlap with training, including 30.0% of records retained after lexical filtering. We therefore used lineage-disjoint partitions. Twelve encoders, comprising three seeds each of Bio-ClinicalBERT, MentalBERT, MentalRoBERTa, and RoBERTa-base, underwent cross-fitted validation for calibration and ensemble selection. A class-specific Complementarity Index (CI), defined as the Jaccard distance between members' correctly classified validation sets, was assessed against independent fusion gain. CI correlated with gain for depression (r=0.50) and suicidal ideation (r=0.68), but not anxiety; results for schizophrenia were mixed. The selected MentalBERT, MentalRoBERTa, and RoBERTa-base triad achieved macro-F1 0.844 [0.823, 0.863], MCC 0.779, and ECE 0.0033 after post-fusion recalibration, improving macro-F1 by 0.021 [0.007, 0.037] over the validation-selected best single encoder. Integrated-Gradients attribution diversity was 2.3 times greater in fusion-rescued cases. Removing divergence-driving words destroyed 58% of rescues, versus 12% under random removal. These findings show that lineage auditing detects dependencies missed by lexical filtering, while class-specific complementarity and post-fusion calibration reveal ensemble behavior obscured by aggregate accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Wadii Boulila, Giuseppe Varone, Bilel Benjdira, Maha Driss

item.title: Omni-Workspace: Benchmarking Omni-Modal AI Assistants on Multimodal Workspace Tasks
item.description: Omni-modal agents are expected to move beyond multimodal understanding toward completing complex tasks in realistic multimodal environments. In these settings, information is distributed across heterogeneous files and modalities, with cross-file and cross-modal dependencies requiring agents to continually coordinate perception, reasoning, and tool use as newly gathered evidence informs subsequent actions. However, existing omni-modal benchmarks primarily focus on multimodal perception and understanding, leaving complex task completion through sustained interaction with multimodal workspaces underexplored. We introduce Omni-Workspace, a benchmark comprising 380 deep-research-style tasks across four multimodal workspace types and two difficulty levels. These tasks require agents to inspect and process workspace files, retrieve external information when needed, integrate evidence across files and modalities, and produce artifacts satisfying explicit requirements. Evaluating 18 representative models reveals limitations in long-horizon multimodal workspace execution, with the best model scoring only 65.93 on average. Further analysis identifies multimodal context inflation and task-state drift as recurring challenges. Motivated by these findings, we further propose OmniFocus, a lightweight approach combining multimodal working-memory management with explicit task-state tracking to improve performance and efficiency. Omni-Workspace advances the evaluation and development of omni-modal agents toward autonomous completion of complex tasks in multimodal workspaces.
item.dc:creator: Yuhao Wang, Yucheng Zhao, Yiran Zhong, Feida Zhu, Hongcheng Liu, Qichao Wang, Ming Ma, Yu Wang

item.title: A Bag of Concepts? Testing Role-Filler Binding in the Verbalizable Workspace
item.description: Runtime alignment monitors built on a verbalizable workspace have been proposed as a way to surface a model's silent cognition before it produces output. Their value rests on the workspace carrying enough structure to distinguish safety-relevant propositions, most of which are relational: "the model plans to deceive the user" and "the user plans to deceive the model" share a concept set and differ only in role assignment. We ask whether the workspace carries the role-filler bindings (which entity fills which role) such a monitor would need, on three frontier language models (Qwen3.6-27B, Gemma-3-12B, Gemma-3-27B-IT), under two lens families (J-lens and R-lens), and with two methods for fitting the role direction (difference-of-means and LRE-gradient). We find a clean dissociation: the workspace carries directions that steer what the model outputs about roles but not the representations the model uses to compute them. Linear probes recover role at near-ceiling from the residual stream but score below a rank-matched random control when reading the workspace, and steering the model along the fitted role direction changes which entity it binds to no more than strength-matched control edits do. Ablating the workspace (zeroing the residual stream's projection onto its ten most active lens directions) damages binding on one of the three models (Gemma-3-27B-IT, holding across three lens variants) and shows no binding-specific damage on the other two, with a rank-matched random subspace as the control; this confirms our design detects binding when present, though scale and instruction tuning are confounded there. A workspace-lens monitor built on these directions would therefore miss a role assignment the model itself represents.
item.dc:creator: Reya Dawlah, Elizabeth McMillin, Michael Shihong Zhang, Badrish Ananth, Rishi Adi Ruia, Ane Zu\~niga, Thomas Jiralerspong

item.title: A Systematic Study of Cross-Token Transfer for Data-Efficient Non-Verbal Text-to-Speech
item.description: Non-verbal vocalizations (NVs), such as laughter and breath, carry affective cues that words alone do not convey. Yet NV data remains scarce because speech annotation pipelines often omit or normalize these events. Existing work has improved NV text-to-speech through model design and data curation, but whether one NV token can help a model learn another has received little systematic study. We investigate this cross-token transferability in a controlled CosyVoice 2 setup. We first trace a laughter-only scaling curve, then hold laughter at 200 or 1,600 examples while adding breath, sigh, cough, lip-smack, or neutral speech. With only 200 laughter examples, adding 3,200 cough examples raises end-to-end laughter F1 from 0.170 to 0.529, surpassing the 0.495 obtained from 1,600 laughter examples alone. At the 1,600-example anchor, cough reaches 0.695, nearly matching 6,400 laughter examples (0.697). Waveform-level Whisper-D scoring and a semantic-token transcriber show consistent trends. Cross-token transfer therefore offers a complementary route to low-resource NV generation.
item.dc:creator: Jing Pan, Haibin Wu, Minxue Niu, Florian Metze, Yuzong Liu

item.title: Low-Latency LLM-Based Streaming Multi-Talker ASR with Verifiable Rewards
item.description: LLM-based architectures offer strong generalization and instruction-following capabilities for streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR), but multi-talker use introduces coupled transcription, attribution, and latency challenges. Our wearable setting requires real-time transcription of a conversation between a near-field device wearer and a far-field partner. Because partial hypotheses are rendered on persistent sides of a dialogue UI, speaker roles cannot be permuted and each speaker tag must precede its turn. These sparse tags are weakly optimized by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while committing to a leading tag can delay the text that follows. We therefore post-train a streaming LLM-based ASR model with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), combining a fixed-role Speaker-Attributed WER (SA-WER) grader with a turn-level onset-delay reward. On an eight-direction multi-talker cohort, SA-WER RL reduces SA-WER from $20.51\%$ for SFT to $13.14\%$. Adding the delay objective reduces onset $p50$ by $65\%$ (from $0.918\,\text{s}$ to $0.320\,\text{s}$) and $p90$ by $44\%$ (from $1.389\,\text{s}$ to $0.780\,\text{s}$) relative to SA-WER-only RL, while achieving $12.70\%$ SA-WER. These results demonstrate that fixed-role recognition quality and streaming responsiveness can be improved jointly.
item.dc:creator: Jing Pan, Ruizhi Li, Ju Lin, Jing Zheng, Florian Metze

item.title: What Transfers Across Cuneiform? Script-Level Substrate and Language-Specific Regularities via Segmentation and Representation
item.description: Cuneiform recorded typologically unrelated languages for more than three millennia, raising a natural question: which of its statistical regularities are properties of the shared writing system, and which belong to individual languages? We answer this with two probe pairs targeting the same script-versus-language decomposition. The first compares two unsupervised, dictionary-free segmentation methods: transitional probability (TP), grounded in infant statistical-learning research, and Morfessor. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic evaluation of dictionary-free segmentation on cuneiform; the only prior published baseline relies on a hand-built dictionary (Max-Match, F1 = 0.74). Both our methods reach F1 > 0.97 within language (Morfessor reaches F1 > 0.99 on Akkadian and Sumerian), exceeding MaxMatch by more than 23 F1 points, but diverge sharply in cross-language transfer: TP holds F1 > 0.95 across all six language pairs, while Morfessor collapses to F1 = 0.27 from the 13K-token Elamite source. A learning curve and a Hittite stress test (34.7% foreign-script logograms, where TP drops 35 points and Morfessor only 8) further isolate the two underlying mechanisms. The second probe pair extends the same decomposition to representations: concatenating Unicode and Latin features improves classification in 11 of 12 morphosyntactic tasks (p < 0.01). We release CUNEI-TOOLS and a three-language benchmark.
item.dc:creator: Chuanjun Zhou, Adam G Anderson

item.title: Beyond Binary Audits: Does Guideline Grounding Mitigate Decision-Space Framing in LLM Opioid Prescribing?
item.description: Audits of LLMs for bias in opioid prescribing have largely relied on binary treatment decisions, a signal that current models have saturated. We introduce Q-Pain++, a full-factorial stress test that holds clinical content fixed while independently varying clinical risk factors and the granularity of the available dosage options. Adding an intermediate dosage option to otherwise unchanged vignettes substantially lowers agreement with expert-annotated dosages for most models, while demographic differences in dosage decisions remain small in all but one configuration once clinical risk factors are added. Grounding models in perioperative guidelines through retrieval reduces this framing effect on average but does not eliminate it, and one model's treatment decisions change when the retrieved passages are reordered. These results suggest that audits should vary the answer format, not only patient identity. We will release our codebase as well as Guideline-RAG-associated resources on GitHub (https://github.com/su-boussard-lab/llm-guideline-grounding-opioids).
item.dc:creator: Soumyadeep Roy, Keyi Yu, Tina Hernandez-Boussard

item.title: Assisting Patients with Reliable Information Gathering: A Guide to Building Efficient QA Systems for Medical Use
item.description: The application of question-answering (QA) systems in the medical domain has rapidly advanced, significantly improving patients' access to reliable health-related information. However, current approaches face notable challenges, including the difficulty in obtaining large-scale and unbiased medical datasets, significant privacy concerns, and inefficiencies due to manual dataset annotation. To address these issues, This study introduce a novel methodology leveraging publicly accessible online health forums to systematically build an unbiased, privacy-conscious QA dataset, and it employs Topic-guided Semantic Modeling (TGSM) for automated topic identification, enabling efficient and targeted annotation of relevant patient-generated content. Subsequently, this study propose a two-stage QA pipeline based on a Retriever-Reader architecture, which is further enhanced through fine-tuning state-of-the-art transformer-based models on the constructed domain-specific QA dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our fine-tuned BioBERT significantly outperforms existing benchmarks, offering accurate patient-derived insights and providing a replicable framework for building efficient medical QA systems.
item.dc:creator: Zhipeng Yin, Zichong Wang, Min Chen, Ian Stockwell, Xin Ning, Jun Liu, Wenbin Zhang

item.title: Self-Evolving Dual-Role Deliberation for Medication Recommendation from Clinical Records
item.description: Recommending medications from electronic health records (EHRs) is a safety-critical task that demands therapeutic coverage, explicit safety constraints, traceable justification, and continual adaptivity. Supervised neural models freeze at deployment and cannot reason about new phenotypes, while existing LLM pipelines are single-pass and lack a cross-case improvement loop. We propose SEMPA, a training-free agentic framework that couples a Proposer with a Critic in multi-round adversarial deliberation, grounds candidates with molecular-aware retrieval, contrastively evolves both agents' natural-language policies under a semantic-anchor constraint, and enforces rule-based DDI and contraindication checks. On 100 MIMIC-IV encounters, SEMPA reaches 0.3116 Jaccard, 0.7295 F1, and a 0.0172 DDI rate, improving F1 by 57.7% and cutting DDI by 77.5% over the strongest supervised baseline. Two LLM judges rank SEMPA highest, and six-backbone studies confirm that gains derive from the framework rather than a specific model.
item.dc:creator: Jiyue Jiang, Yu Lei, Yitao Xu, Zikang Wang, Zhenyu Wang, Licheng Zong, Han Huang, Ziyi Li, Zhiyu Huo, Yuhan Chen, Jiayang Chen, Xiaodan Fan, Yu Li

item.title: Automating literature screening and knowledge synthesis with large language models
item.description: Scientific literature is expanding rapidly, yet much of its knowledge remains difficult to organize and reuse due to the substantial workload needed to navigate large, heterogeneous literature corpora. Here, we develop a generalizable large language model (LLM)-powered framework that automates literature screening, structured information extraction, and knowledge synthesis within a unified workflow. We benchmarked 11 state-of-the-art proprietary and open-weight LLMs across three materials science screening tasks differing in scope, corpus size, and class imbalance. Seven LLMs achieved balanced accuracies above 0.90 across all tasks, with the best-performing LLM reaching 0.96--0.98, demonstrating the potential of LLMs to accurately screen large, highly imbalanced scientific corpora. The framework also substantially reduces manual effort, screening 10,000 records within four minutes compared with approximately 83 person-hours for manual screening. Beyond literature screening, the framework extracts structured information from full-text articles, enabling content-level quantification of research landscapes that extends traditional bibliometric analysis based on publication metadata. This capability reveals methodological trends and underexplored directions, as shown for machine learning in concrete materials science. We further demonstrate its utility for information and data discovery by identifying publications containing silicate glass density data that are difficult to retrieve using conventional search strategies, which can support downstream hypothesis development, research design, and data-driven scientific discovery. Overall, these results demonstrate the broad applicability of LLM-powered literature analysis across scientific domains and its potential to transform large, unstructured literature corpora into structured, analyzable knowledge at scale.
item.dc:creator: Zhanzhao Li, Qiyao He, Weiqiang Chen, Kengran Yang, Kai Gong

item.title: Human vs Machine Translation Detection: A Cross-Model, Cross-Domain, and Low-Resource Analysis
item.description: The growing reliance on web-crawled corpora for training large language models introduces a critical challenge: machine-translated (MT) content is often treated as human translation (HT), potentially degrading data quality and propagating synthetic artifacts, especially in low-resource settings. In this work, we study MT-HT detectability across high-resource (English, Spanish) and low-resource (Swahili, Afrikaans) languages using both decoder-only LLMs in zero-shot and few-shot settings, and fine-tuned multilingual encoders trained at the sentence level and on token-chunked inputs. We find that decoder-only models provide limited discrimination overall and exhibit a consistent class-asymmetric failure mode: they recognize human-written text reliably (high HT recall) but rarely flag fluent machine output (low MT recall). Encoder-based classifiers achieve high accuracy when evaluated on data generated by the same MT systems and translators used during training in a legislative domain, but their MT recall drops sharply on unseen translators and on unseen domains such as low-resource conversational text and medical content. To address this limitation, we evaluate models on longer inputs by chunking text into segments of up to 300 tokens, which substantially improves generalization, suggesting that sentence-level signals are insufficient for robust detection. Finally, we analyze the relationship between translation quality and detectability using COMET and BLEURT, showing that lower-quality MT is more easily identified, while high-quality MT remains difficult to distinguish from HT. Our results highlight the importance of input granularity, translator generalization, and translation quality in building robust MT detection systems across domains and languages.
item.dc:creator: Yabsera Yemanberhan, Prasenjit Mitra, Roald Eiselen

item.title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models
item.description: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.
item.dc:creator: Paul-Andrei Sava, Alexander K\"uchler, Daniel Kowatsch, Bernhard Grill, Jennifer Pullman, Yanick Fratantonio, Luca Invernizzi

item.title: Agent-Native by Design: A Programming Language for Agentic Applications
item.description: Building agentic applications requires combining large language model (LLM) operations, workflow structure and application state, and model-guided routing. With SDKs and agent frameworks, developers connect these components through supporting code that prepares model inputs, propagates state, and dispatches model-selected steps. Workflow changes can require coordinated updates to this code, increasing development and testing effort. Splitting execution logic between application code and framework internals also limits compiler visibility into control flow and state dependencies, hindering automatic optimization. We introduce Agent-Native Programming, which unifies these three components with shared execution semantics. We realize this approach in Jac, a Python-superset language, through "by llm()" for typed model operations and tool use, Object-Spatial Programming for workflow structure and state, and "visit ... by llm()" for model-guided routing. The routing construct derives the model's choices from executable workflow steps and schedules the selected steps. This explicit connection between model decisions and program execution gives the compiler and runtime a common basis for dependency analysis and automatic optimization. Across five benchmarks and five baselines, Jac achieves a 1.8-8.7x reduction in AI-integration code relative to the OpenAI SDK, with competitive observed task quality and lower coding-agent development effort. Two case studies demonstrate speculative execution and service partitioning through configuration alone, using program analysis and runtime checks to preserve workflow behavior under stated conditions.
item.dc:creator: Jayanaka Dantanarayana, Savini Kashmira, Xiaoyu Ma, Malitha, Malitha Prabhashana, Lingjia Tang, Jason Mars

item.title: Human-AI Co-Ideation Across Socio-Technical Configurations: An Interactional Analysis of Planar and Immersive Workspaces
item.description: Remote collaborative platforms increasingly integrate generative AI to support group ideation. These platforms are sociotechnical configurations in which spatial mediation, interaction modality, AI output format, and the mechanisms that make contributions visible to a group co-vary as properties of a deployed system. This paper examines how such configurations shape participants' collaboration and their engagement with AI during creative work. We report a comparative study of two commercially available platforms that instantiate contrasting configurations: a planar shared canvas with text-based AI integration, and an immersive virtual reality workspace with concise AI output embedded in the shared space. Fourteen all-women triads completed a structured ideation task consisting of human-only idea generation, AI-supported idea expansion, and group convergence. We analyzed collaboration patterns, selection of AI-generated ideas, perceived idea quality, workload, presence, and their lexical characteristics. The immersive configuration yielded greater spatial presence and introduced a participation paradox, in which spatial freedom enabled exploration and fragmented group coherence; it was also associated with more balanced role distribution during convergence, at the cost of higher physical demand. In both configurations, AI multiplied the idea pool, and ideas groups authored with AI available were rated above participants' own. AI output format: about 21 words per idea on the planar canvas and 3 in the immersive workspace. Tracked how participants evaluated AI-generated ideas and how often they selected them unaltered as finalists. Neither configuration made AI contributions visible or attributable to the group: participants invoked AI individually and asynchronously in both. We derive design implications for AI output format, group-visible AI invocation, and spatial support for convergence

item.title: What Makes a Good Move? Learning to Act from Experience in Visual Worlds
item.description: Learning visual policies requires turning interaction experience into guidance for individual decisions. Trajectory outcomes obscure action quality, while unguided exploration can revisit familiar situations. We present \textsc{LightAct}, an experience-learning framework that connects skill-guided exploration with policy internalization. Interaction segments are summarized into experience entries and consolidated into a game-specific skill that guides root collection toward broader state coverage. At each root, candidate actions are compared through short rollouts under a shared frozen policy. Environment-reported score gains are averaged across continuations and normalized into relative action rewards, producing reusable supervision for reinforcement learning. Policy training uses a compact dataset of just 1,024 decision roots collected in a single source game and paired with their action rewards. Across 170 GameWorld tasks spanning 34 games, \textsc{LightAct} improves overall progress by 23.6, 29.2, and 13.0 percentage points at the 2B, 4B, and 9B scales, respectively, with our strongest model competitive with reported proprietary-model results. Ablations show broader root-state coverage with skill guidance and consistent gains across three policy optimizers. Case studies show how rollouts distinguish actions with identical immediate gains.
item.dc:creator: Cehao Yang, Ziyi He, Jing Yi, Jian Guo, Hui Xiong

item.title: Experience Rot: Experienced Agents Fail Where Novices Succeed
item.description: Agents are increasingly built to learn from experience: they keep conversation histories, memory files, retrieved notes and skills, and reuse what worked before. We show that this experience turns against them when their tools change silently. We test a range of models with tools defined as in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). After a silent change, experienced agents fail on most tasks, while agents new to the task mostly succeed. We call this failure Experience Rot. Experienced agents copy their earlier call instead of checking the current interface, even when the tool definition shows the change. Then they report success. When the documentation is incomplete, experience is what makes agents succeed. After a change, the same experience leaves them worse off than no experience at all. The failure appears in every form of memory we test and grows with the amount of experience. Simple remedies fall short: announcing the update barely helps, and pointing the agent to the documentation fails whenever the documentation does not spell out the answer.
item.dc:creator: Zhen Xu, Hang Yin, Zitao Zhang, Kevin Zhao, Xuefeng Liu

item.title: Re-Reading Is Not Free: Token Traces and Cache-Aware Energy Estimation for LLM Agents in Software Engineering
item.description: As large language models (LLMs) evolve from conversational assistants into autonomous agents embedded in software development workflows, estimating their environmental footprint requires moving beyond conventional token-based accounting. Existing energy estimators focus on isolated request-response interactions, overlooking the repeated processing of accumulated context, cache reuse, and work delegated to subagents. We analyze nearly one billion tokens collected across 42 sessions and 752 task episodes over ten weeks of real-world AI-assisted software development. Cached-context reads make up 94.8% of all API-reported tokens, while uncached input accounts for only 0.017%; for every generated token, approximately 260 cached tokens are read. Context grows 5.3-fold over a session compared with 1.4-fold within individual tasks. To quantify the energy implications, we extend an existing analytical inference-energy model to account for cached-context processing, yielding a cache-aware hybrid estimator. It estimates approximately 250 kWh for the workload, compared with approximately 10 kWh from the output-based estimator EcoLogits, a 25-fold difference largely driven by cached-context reads. Neither estimator has been validated on long cached contexts, but no modeling assumption we varied closes the gap. Starting each task from a fresh context would lower our estimate by about 60%. We also find that parent-session logs report only a subagent's final internal call, undercounting delegated tokens by a factor of ten; for this workload the correction changes the energy estimate by about 5%, but token-volume studies are fully exposed to it. Our findings expose a substantial gap between how current energy estimators and agentic workloads treat context, highlighting the need for workflow-level energy accounting that captures context accumulation, cache reuse, and delegated execution.

item.title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
item.description: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.

item.title: Memory-Efficient Speculative Decoding with Quantized Draft KV Cache
item.description: Speculative decoding reduces generation cost, but it stores two KV caches: one for the target model and one for the draft model. We reduce this extra memory by quantizing the draft cache. The target cache and verifier remain in BF16, so that compression cannot change the target model's final correction rule. We first study how to divide precision between keys and values. A naive per-token quantizer makes keys appear much more sensitive: splitting a 12-bit budget, K8V4 beats K4V8 in acceptance by 10.87pp. However, with grouped per-channel keys, the gap becomes -0.25pp. A controlled Qwen test confirms that changing only the key quantizer can erase or reverse the preferred bit split. Hence, following KIVI, we propose K4V4 quantization with per-channel keys and per-token values. Across six model pairs, our method reduces draft cache memory by 66.20%, and combined memory across both caches by 23.95%. Mean acceptance drops from 57.93% to 57.14%, only 1.36% relative. Overall, quantized draft caches can make speculative decoding more memory efficient; as a predictive principle for efficient AI design, key and value precision must be co-designed with the quantizer layout.
item.dc:creator: Saksham Gupta, Michael Li

item.title: One-Shot Calibration via Model Editing
item.description: Model editing aims to correct errors in large, pretrained models by replacing model generations with user-provided responses. Existing editors assume a single target answer for each edit. However, many real tasks inherently entail uncertainty, resulting in multiple plausible answers with varying likelihoods in user feedback. Such feedback forms a target distribution to not only correct but also calibrate model generations. We therefore propose SoftEdit, the first model editor to leverage uncertainty in user responses and perform one-shot calibration during editing. To generalize calibration to unseen samples, SoftEdit uses co-plausibility relationships between answers while preserving real distributional shifts, balancing the new distributional generality-locality tradeoff. Across three language models, three vision-language models, and two large datasets, SoftEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance, ultimately showing that uncertainty in user responses enables generalizable calibration of pretrained models beyond single-answer corrections.
item.dc:creator: Jiaxing Qiu, Luke Hakso, Roxana Daneshjou, Ahmed Alaa, Thomas Hartvigsen

item.title: Making Koopman Control Guarantees Hold on Robots
item.description: A Koopman controller can stabilize its learned latent-space linear model yet fail to stabilize the nonlinear plant. The learned model propagates predictions in latent space, while the deployed controller repeatedly re-encodes the measured physical state. We show that nominal closed-loop stability transfers to the nonlinear plant when the learned and true closed-loop dynamics agree to first order on the embedding's tangent space at the target. We derive a robustness margin for approximate matching and show that a stable open-loop latent model cannot exactly match an unstable equilibrium. We introduce Tangent-Invariant Koopman (TIK), which estimates a local plant linearization from offline transitions and enforces first-order matching to this estimate. TIK recovers the fitted LQR gain at the target, while a bilinear predictor captures state-dependent actuation during large maneuvers. Across four simulated unstable benchmarks, all 40 Standard Koopman controllers have stable latent closed loops, but their deployed nonlinear systems are locally unstable. In contrast, all 40 TIK controllers locally stabilize their respective nonlinear plants. An offline stability test using empirical curvature estimates identifies stable TIK controllers on two cart-pole systems, but is inconclusive under high noise. Under explicit model-error and curvature bounds, an invariant terminal set guarantees constraint satisfaction after entry under local feedback. TIK achieves 88\% constrained cart-pole swing-up success with a 0.25 ms planning budget and controls simulated seven-joint arms within 1-5 ms per step.
item.dc:creator: Abulikemu Abuduweili, Changliu Liu

item.title: Pretty Linear Liars: Unregularized Probes Favor Intervention-Unfaithful Features
item.description: Linear probing is a common technique in mechanistic interpretability despite the fact that the decodability of a given feature does not necessarily imply the network uses that feature. Intervention faithfulness, not merely decodability, is the appropriate criterion for whether a feature serves a defined active role in the model. Meanwhile, probe regularization has been used for feature discovery, but the impact of regularization on feature causality remains unclear. We study probe regularization systematically, starting with unregularized ordinary least squares (OLS) regression and considering increasing amounts of regularization via ridge regression. We show theoretically that OLS probes amplify low-variance directions in activation space that have spurious correlations with the target feature, whereas regularization reduces influence from these directions. Empirically, we find in a toy transformer and Llama-2-7B that intervention faithfulness increases up to a point, and then decreases again, and that the optimal regularization strength leads to features bearing striking similarity (in both direction and variance) to those learned by optimizing for intervention outcomes directly. Together, these results provide mechanistic justification for regularizing regression probes.
item.dc:creator: Karl Vilhelmsson Emneby, Julian Yocum, Cameron Allen

item.title: Benchmarking LLM Inference on Desktop-Scale NVIDIA Grace Blackwell Clusters
item.description: Two NVIDIA DGX Spark GB10 systems connect directly over 200 GbE to serve larger language models and increase inference capacity, but the benefits depend on how they are deployed. We benchmark 17 open-weight checkpoints spanning dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, 8B to 235B parameters and four weight precisions on one and two RDMA-connected systems. Using vLLM, we compare tensor parallelism (TP=2), pipeline parallelism (PP=2) and a two-replica baseline at concurrency 1 to 64, with three independent launches per configuration. TP=2 delivers a median 1.59x peak-throughput gain over one Spark, versus 1.39x for PP=2 and has higher throughput in 93 of 96 matched comparisons with separated 95% Welch intervals. It reduces unloaded inter-token latency to 0.52x to 0.73x of one Spark, whereas PP=2 provides little reduction. TP=2 also achieves the highest goodput under a strict 100 ms inter-token latency objective wherever both strategies are supported and the objective is met. For models fitting on one Spark, TP=2 generally favors low-concurrency serving, while replication offers higher throughput at high concurrency. One Spark uses less GPU energy per output token at matched concurrency. Across three precision ladders, NVFP4 reduces unloaded latency more than adding a second Spark at BF16. NCCL microbenchmarks and comparisons with an earlier TCP campaign suggest that collective communication overhead contributes to the advantage of TP=2. These results provide deployment guidance for desktop-scale inference.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Bhimani, Christian Escobar, Daniel Mihovch, Rudolf Eigenmann, Sunita Chandrasekaran

item.title: Paying Creators for Training Data Can Increase AI Displacement
item.description: Generative AI increasingly competes with creators while using their content as training data. In response, policymakers have called for platforms to compensate creators for training data use and allow opting out. We study how such policies affect creator displacement in a model of a platform where creators choose whether to contribute training data and consumers choose between purchasing from creators and prompting generative AI trained on their content. When compensation is required, the low-quality creator chooses to remain solely as a training data supplier while AI fully displaces her demand, despite AI quality and the price the platform charges for AI-generated content being identical with and without compensation. Without compensation, the risk of losing creators and their training data constrains the platform to set the price of creators' content to preserve their demand. This constraint also prevents further AI displacement as AI improves, with the platform raising AI prices while keeping creators' prices and demand unchanged to prevent exit. Compensation increases creators' payoffs and total surplus but reduces consumer surplus. Our findings highlight how compensation policies for training data can shape creators' economic roles in a future with more capable generative AI.
item.dc:creator: Lijuan Luo, Emaad Manzoor, Nathan Yang, Fan Yao

item.title: Locational Marginal Pricing of Compute: Co-optimizing Compute and Energy for Transparent Data Center Flexibility
item.description: Demand from data centers and AI compute is growing rapidly and is increasing stress on the power grid. This load could be flexible through user adjustments and provide relief during energy scarcity events, yet today its flexibility is provided through utility call-ups or system-operator load shedding, and is invisible to the users whose workloads are being curtailed. In this work, we propose to quantify and couple the prices of compute and energy in a single optimization problem. The resulting compute price reflects the marginal cost of the binding constraints and decomposes into components indicating which grid, power, hardware, or service requirement causes a price surge. The economic interpretation updates the price with real-time conditions and gives users a signal for potential flexibility provision. The co-optimization ultimately connects compute and energy markets while providing a signal for relief of stress on both the grid and the compute resources.
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Pyltsov, Teng Zeng

item.title: SAFER: Navigating the Exploration-Exploitation Dilemma in World-Model-Based Planning for Autonomous Driving
item.description: An autonomous vehicle must foresee the consequences of its actions, especially in the rare, time-critical situations where crashes happen. A world model offers this foresight, but only within the coverage of its training data, which poses an exploration-exploitation dilemma. Within this coverage a planner can hardly improve on the data, and beyond it the model's errors mislead it. Logs of competent driving rarely contain the failures that would widen the coverage, and agents that learn from interaction gain them only by failing themselves, without being shown what to do instead. We propose SAFER, a framework that learns offline from failures that others make, judged by an expert, and keeps learning online from its own driving. Offline, partially trained agents and scripted, recoverable perturbations Stage failures in simulation, and an expert Annotates every visited state with its action and value, so that much of what the planner explores is covered before it drives. In planning, a chunked latent world model Foresees the consequences fast enough for real-time use, and a risk-aware sampling-based planner Evaluates candidate maneuvers by their return minus a bounded collision penalty. Online, a loop continuously Refines the model wherever this driving leaves the coverage of the offline data. In closed-loop evaluation against the compared methods, SAFER reaches the highest route completion and reward per step on the CARLA Leaderboard routes, 0.95 and 0.77 from a privileged bird's-eye view, and the highest episode reward in MetaDrive, 53.4 in regular and 49.0 in safety-critical traffic. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/safer-website.
item.dc:creator: Yansong Qu, Zilin Huang, Zihao Sheng, Sikai Chen, Samuel Labi

item.title: The Flip Test: Video World Models Fail to Learn the World State
item.description: Video world models promise to predict the future of a scene from its present. Do current models keep this promise? We probe this question counterfactually. When a small change to the present flips the future, such as a box resting a few millimeters before or past a table edge, a model that tracks the state of the world must flip its prediction too. We build FlipTest, a three-level hierarchy of increasingly strict tests over 1,680 initial frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks. At the base, visual minimal pairs, two nearly identical frames whose true futures differ, test whether predictions change across the boundary; matched controls go further and test whether they change only where the future does; and dense sweeps, the strictest level, locate exactly where they change. All 11 video world models we evaluate fall short. The best averages 18.3% pair accuracy over real and simulated scenes, below the 25% of random guessing. Models flip as often on steps that leave the future unchanged as on steps that change it, and their response stays flat across the sweeps. On the same frames, a vision-language model is selective and traces a near S-shaped curve near the boundary, and a coding agent that measures the image comes close to the true boundary. This implies that the deciding information is in the frame, and video models just miss it. We therefore urge the community to rethink world modeling as pure video prediction. Next-frame prediction must do more than draw plausible pixels; it must also identify the causal states that control future dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Mi Luo, Lijun Yu, Adams Wei Yu, Ang Cao, Baochen Sun, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Nan Hua, Yuan Hao, Alex Dimakis, Ya Xu, Ed H. Chi, Xuezhi Wang, Yinxiao Liu

item.title: Where Should LLM Agents Adapt at Test Time? In Context, in Weights, or Both
item.description: LLM agents operating repeatedly in the same environment, such as a code repository, a database, or an application suite, encounter tasks that share latent structure. Experience can reveal this structure, allowing agents to reuse environment knowledge and learn from environmental feedback. Agents can adapt at test-time using this experience through two channels: retaining it in context and updating their weights. These channels are usually studied separately, leaving unclear what each contributes and when they complement each other. We compare in-context learning (ICL), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards using GRPO, and self-distillation using SDPO, alone and in combination, using a shared online protocol and modular framework. Agents encounter matched task streams, are evaluated on each task before adapting to it, and learn only from their own attempts and environment feedback. We evaluate 14 adaptation mechanisms and a stateless baseline with Qwen3.5-9B on 109 tasks from four environments drawn from SWE-bench Verified, AppWorld, ScienceWorld, and BIRD-Critic-SQLite, using five task orders per environment. ICL provides the largest standalone gain: its best policy raises mean success across environments from 28.8% to 49.4%. Adding GRPO to this policy achieves the highest mean success, 51.6%. While adding GRPO improves the overall mean under every ICL policy, SDPO has mixed effects. Trace analyses show fewer lookups and shorter attempts under ICL, consistent with reusing knowledge of the shared structure. However, ICL also frequently skips inspection and verification for the current task. Adding GRPO to ICL helps restore these behaviors while preserving its reduced environment lookups. These observations suggest that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can refine how agents use retained experience, motivating the joint study of context management and weight updates.
item.dc:creator: Parsa Mirtaheri, Mohammadreza Armandpour, Keivan Alizadeh, Iman Mirzadeh, Parshin Shojaee, Aryo Lotfi, David Harrison, Mehrdad Farajtabar

item.title: Data Attribution Should Steer Pretraining
item.description: Pretraining data curation decides what a model learns from, yet what makes a document worth learning from depends on what the model already knows. Influence-driven selectors already rank documents to improve one run; we argue that training-data attribution should steer pretraining by identifying testable data properties that become reusable curation criteria, evaluated on new data against cheaper selectors at matched total cost, discovery included. A document ranking is consumed by the run it was computed for, whereas an explained data property can be tested across corpora and checkpoints, especially where familiar quality signals diverge from measured usefulness. Because historical contribution, an understandable explanation, and future data value require distinct evidence, we specify a feedback loop that interprets attributed sources, tests candidate data changes, and states for five claim types what evidence each requires and what none establishes. We close with a falsifiable comparison against perplexity, classifier, and mixing baselines at equal total compute.
item.dc:creator: Glenn Matlin, Chandreyi Chakraborty, Mohammed Rehan Parwani, Saehee Eom, Anthony Wen-Ming Zang, Akhil Theerthala, Arjun Chatterjee, Tejas Khandwekar, Brandon Michaels, Alvin Deng, Mark Riedl

item.title: BadGCL: Towards Persistent Backdoor Attack on Graph Continual Learning Systems
item.description: Backdoor attacks pose a persistent security threat to machine learning systems, yet their behavior under graph continual learning (GCL) remains underexplored. Conventional graph backdoor attacks often lose effectiveness as models are updated across successive tasks, creating the impression that continual updates naturally weaken malicious associations. This work reveals a contrasting vulnerability: knowledge-preservation mechanisms in GCL can also preserve early injected backdoors when the poisoned update is compatible with the clean-task signal being retained. For graph data, this risk is amplified by structural triggers, which are embedded into the message-passing paths of graph neural networks (GNNs) and can induce stable representation shifts across tasks. To expose this risk, we propose BadGCL, a model-agnostic framework for persistent backdoor attacks under a strict early-stage intervention setting. BadGCL learns topology-aware structural triggers using a gradient mutual-information objective that couples poisoned gradients with clean-task optimization signals, together with a propagation consistency objective that stabilizes trigger-induced effects through graph message passing. We provide theoretical analysis showing that gradient compatibility and propagation stability jointly support long-term backdoor persistence under benign continual updates. Extensive experiments across task-IL and class-IL protocols, four GCL benchmarks, and diverse victim systems show that BadGCL achieves persistent attack effectiveness with limited clean-utility degradation, substantially outperforming graph and continual-learning backdoor baselines and remaining robust against representative defenses.
item.dc:creator: Dong Li, Yufei Han, Xintao Wu, Xujiang Zhao, Wei Cheng, Chen Zhao

item.title: ROUNDS: Source-Framed Diagnostic Revision after Multi-Turn Clinical Evidence
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on medical benchmarks, but does this performance translate into reliable diagnosis as a conversation unfolds? In diagnostic conversations, users can provide clinical findings across multiple turns, ask for a diagnosis without supplying answer options, and introduce opinions from others. Models must therefore form diagnoses from the available evidence and decide how to respond to subsequent advice. We introduce ROUNDS, a framework that evaluates these abilities after a fixed sequence of clinical evidence delivered over multiple turns. ROUNDS compares diagnosis with and without answer options, presents the same incorrect diagnosis under clinician and lay framing, and varies support for competing diagnoses in written five-clinician panels. Across seven models and 1,035 cases from five datasets, average accuracy was 76.9% with answer options and 57.0% without them. Clinician-framed misleading advice produced lower final accuracy than lay-framed advice in every model, with differences of 4.6 to 38.2 percentage points. Initially correct diagnoses more often became incorrect answers than abstentions, and many adopted the suggested disease. Conversely, accuracy increased as more panel members supported the correct diagnosis, including when the majority opinion remained unchanged. These findings reveal a gap between medical benchmark performance and reliable diagnosis in conversation: models respond to external opinions, but remain vulnerable to abandoning correct diagnoses without new clinical evidence.
item.dc:creator: Jinrui Fang, Runhan Chen, Yining Wu, Jiawei Xu, Xu Yang, Jian Yu, Wenqi Shi, Ying Ding, Yuji Zhang

item.title: PBit1: One Programmable P-Bit per Parameter - A Finite-Control Representation of Pretrained Networks
item.description: We introduce PBit1, a finite-control representation of pretrained neural networks that assigns one programmable p-bit to each learned parameter. A 12-bit command sets its probability, a shared affine range maps that probability to the weight domain, and temporal observations reconstruct the weight for inference. Operator-aware range grouping and sensitivity-based sampling allocation adapt the representation to the network. Across five independent weight draws at 32,768 observations per scalar, selected configurations preserve task quality in GPT-2, DistilBERT, and LFM3-1.7B with every learned scalar converted and no fine-tuning. GPT-2 and LFM3 perplexity increase by approximately 0.66% and 0.26%, respectively, while DistilBERT accuracy changes from 87.51% to 87.49%. A sensitivity-based policy reduces GPT-2 reconstruction observations by 41.7% while retaining the quality criterion. Complete-model evaluations reuse reconstructed weights in BF16 inference, and THRML operator experiments examine native sampling and spatial-temporal tradeoffs. Together, these results establish PBit1 as a concrete construction for studying finite-control weight representation and temporal reconstruction in pretrained networks.
item.dc:creator: Omar Ramadan

item.title: Do Pretraining Optimizer Gains Transfer to KL Distillation?
item.description: Matrix-structured optimizers can improve language-model pretraining, but it is unclear whether these gains transfer to short-horizon KL distillation from an instruction-tuned initialization. We compare AdamW and diagonal AdaGrad with two tractable Shampoo reductions, SOAP, and All-2D Muon across four dense Qwen student-teacher pairs under a common forward-KL objective and fixed training budget. Across scales, none of the evaluated matrix-structured recipes consistently improves the quality versus trainer-time trade-off over the elementwise references: AdamW generally attains the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be slightly faster at larger scale. SOAP often tracks AdamW in KL but incurs substantial trainer-time overhead, and the two Shampoo reductions reverse ordering across model pairs, showing that conclusions depend on the feasible recipe. These results suggest that pretraining optimizer gains do not transfer automatically to KL distillation and should be re-established for the target objective and systems regime.
item.dc:creator: Lavinia Ghita, Dhruv Desai

item.title: OmitEHR: Scalable Omission Detection in LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries
item.description: Health systems increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to draft summaries of patient medical records, yet evaluations now find omissions, the absence of clinically important information, to be the most common failure mode. Detecting omissions in an LLM-generated summary requires knowing which facts in the record are salient, a signal that existing methods hand-specify, ignore, or recompute at inference with costly LLM judges. We present OmitEHR, a reference-free omission detector that learns clinical salience from historical clinician-written summaries predating widespread LLM use. OmitEHR learns to predict which source-note sentences clinicians include in their summaries, then surfaces high-salience sentences not covered by an LLM-generated summary as candidate omissions. We apply OmitEHR to brief hospital course (BHC) summarization using 5,000 admissions from a large academic medical center. On held-out admissions, OmitEHR outperformed all evaluated baselines at predicting salient source sentences, including a prompted LLM judge. The full omission detection pipeline took 17.7 to 19.5 seconds and cost \$0.03 to \$0.13 per summary depending on the base model, 1.6 to 1.7 times faster and 5.6 to 6.7 times cheaper than scoring every source sentence with an LLM judge. In a blinded review of 25 admissions, two board-certified clinicians confirmed a mean of 5.6 clinically meaningful omissions per summary surfaced by OmitEHR, compared with 3.3 for a full LLM pipeline, counting candidates confirmed by at least one clinician. The efficiency and validity of OmitEHR make it a practical tool for health systems to flag omissions before a summary reaches the clinician.
item.dc:creator: Bridget Lin, Ryan Welch, Bobak Seddighzadeh, Fran Riley, Kaitlyn Stoehr, Margarita I. Pipinos, Dimitri Speron, Emma V. Sage, Sneha Jain, Nigam H. Shah, Emily Alsentzer

item.title: Benchmarking the State of AI for Crop Yield Forecasting: A Global Assessment Across Modeling Paradigms
item.description: Accurate crop yield forecasting is essential for food security, agricultural policy, and commodity markets. Although statistical, process-based, and machine learning approaches have all been proposed, their relative strengths remain poorly understood due to the lack of large-scale, standardized comparisons. We address this gap through a comprehensive benchmark of five modeling paradigms -- statistical baselines, process-based models, conventional feature-engineered machine learning, deep sequence models, and tabular foundation models -- using the CY-Bench benchmark spanning 63 country-crop datasets (>12,000 administrative regions) across six continents. Beyond conventional pooled accuracy metrics, we introduce a multi-dimensional evaluation framework that separately quantifies overall, spatial, temporal, and anomaly prediction skill. Across multiple crops and countries, feature-engineered machine learning and tabular foundation models achieve the strongest overall predictive performance. Data-driven models reduce NRMSE in 72% of countries growing maize and 78% of countries growing wheat, with median reductions of 8.8% and 11.9%, respectively. Across all modeling paradigms, spatial prediction is substantially easier than temporal and anomaly prediction. While data-driven models markedly improve temporal and anomaly prediction over statistical baselines, accurately forecasting year-to-year yield variability remains challenging. These findings suggest that future progress in large-scale crop yield forecasting will depend on the improved characterization of the environmental and management factors driving inter-annual yield variability, founded on effective representations for crop yield forecasting systems that support agricultural decision-making, early-warning applications, and food security planning
item.dc:creator: Michiel Kallenberg, Philip Janz, Christoph J\"orges, Vageesh Saxena, Pratishtha Poudel, Mohammed Musthafa Rafi, Ioannis N. Athanasiadis

item.title: HospitalBench: Diagnosing Where and Why Embodied Agents Fail on Long Hospital Task Chains
item.description: Long-horizon embodied tasks fail in ways that end-task success cannot see. HospitalBench is a diagnostic benchmark of ten hospital chores in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, each two unscored warm-up steps followed by a causal chain of five scored sub-tasks in one continuous simulation: the state one step leaves (an object pose, a choice, a fact seen once) determines what the next step must do, unlike benchmarks that place sub-tasks side by side. Vision-language agents act through skill-level tools from camera images. A scripted robot that makes only the calls a model gets is the solvability check of a chore. From each trajectory the benchmark reads where a chain breaks, what the agent did after a failed call, and how far its own position estimate drifts from the true one. This version reports first results only: 15 of 60 planned runs (three models at high effort, one run each on chores T1 and T10 from both start states and T3 from one), with scripted-robot proofs on three of the ten chores. Of the 15 runs, 2 passed all five sub-tasks. Runs still going after sub-tasks 1 to 5 were 15, 8, 4, 2, 2. Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by a different call and 111 by a call that did not fail. These are first results and not a full benchmark. We will release the scenes, task chains, scripted robot, evaluation harness and trajectories.
item.dc:creator: Gaytri Jena, Kapil Wanaskar, Aman Chadha, Vasu Sharma, Vinija Jain, Amitava Das

item.title: On-policy distillation as a Backdoor Propagation Channel
item.description: On-policy distillation (OPD) is emerging as an important paradigm for the post training of large language models, improving student models by leveraging supervision generated online by teacher models. However, whether this process also transfers latent security risks from teacher models to student models remains insufficiently studied. In this work, we reveal a new security risk in which an attacker first implants a conditional backdoor into the teacher model through supervised fine tuning (SFT), after which OPD can transfer the backdoor to the student model with only an extremely small proportion of trigger prompt exposure. More concerningly, we find that such backdoor transfer is substantially stronger under OPD than under conventional distillation methods, suggesting that OPD may provide an efficient channel for propagating backdoors across models. Our mechanistic analysis shows that the backdoor signal is primarily transmitted through anomalous differences in the conditional probabilities produced by the teacher model for triggered and clean inputs, and is gradually internalized into the internal representations of the student model during training. Furthermore, we investigate how to suppress such anomalous conditional probability signals at the source of distillation supervision and, based on this analysis, propose an OPD training method tailored to this conditional backdoor propagation setting to mitigate the risk of backdoor transfer induced by untrusted teacher supervision.
item.dc:creator: Zane Fu, Yanzhao Zheng, Ziting Qin, Qianshan Wei, Yi Yu, Gongli Xi, Jihuai Zhu, Baohua Dong, Hangcheng Zhu, Ruohui Huang, Gang Yu

item.title: Hard or Mislabeled? Failure Screens Enrich Vision Benchmarks for Label Errors
item.description: Hard vision benchmarks often keep images that strong classifiers get wrong. Since a classifier is also marked wrong when the label is wrong, such failure screens may collect label errors. We measure this on ImageNet's twice-relabeled validation set with 103 classifiers. Among the 1,892 images that all 66 supervised classifiers get wrong, 61% have a wrong label, versus 11.1% overall. The fewer images a screen lets through, the more of them are mislabeled, along approximately one curve. Fit on one model family, this curve predicts the screens of two held-out model families with a mean error of 2.4 percentage points, and replays of ImageNet-D's and ImageNet-Hard's screens within 0.1 and 6.3 points. On new pools, ImageNet-V2 and CIFAR-10, enrichment at the strictest screens is stronger than the curve predicts: on ImageNet-V2, by human relabeling, 67% of the images that all 66 classifiers get wrong are mislabeled, against 46% predicted. Screens that let models choose among only some of the classes, as ImageNet-A's does (200 of 1,000), fall below the curve. By ReImageNet, 32% of ImageNet-Hard's ImageNet images have no correct label. ScreenAudit, which comprises an audit tool, a script that rebuilds corrected answer sets for the 5,464 decided ImageNet-Hard images (of 5,646) from ReImageNet's gated release, and per-image audits of 1,198 benchmark images, will be released later.
item.dc:creator: Haolin Guo

item.title: Model Maps: A Documentation Framework for Tracing Foundation Model Ancestry and Understanding AI Entanglement
item.description: The development of foundation models incorporates pre-existing AI artifacts like models, datasets, and benchmarks. These relationships, as part of the broader AI supply chain, produce "entangled" webs in which properties of artifacts upstream can influence the outputs of a foundation model downstream - a phenomenon known as AI entanglement. Without visibility into these connections, a black-box model can inherit upstream properties that result in security vulnerabilities, hallucinations, or biased predictions, yet developers are left with no recourse to identify or mitigate the root issue. To address these concerns, we introduce model maps as a conceptual documentation framework for tracing model ancestry that builds on previous documentation frameworks like ecosystem graphs, datasheets, and model cards. A model map for a given foundation model is a detailed knowledge graph that represents the relationships between artifacts that influence the resulting foundation model. Our framework incorporates a taxonomy of 13 dependency mechanisms including model fine-tuning and synthetic data generation. We apply this framework to construct model maps of 15 closed and open-weight foundation models to illustrate the complexity of AI entanglement in current model development practices. From our model maps, we record 2,778 unique dependencies and trace artifacts that are located up to 9 hops away from a resulting foundation model. Our findings suggest that AI transparency requirements should extend beyond individual models and training-data disclosures to encompass upstream dependencies, which would enable more effective risk assessment, auditing, and accountability across the AI supply chain. To help developers, regulators, and researchers understand and analyze the interactions that can influence the behavior of a foundation model, we release these these model maps at https://modelmaps.ai.
item.dc:creator: Rachel Hong, Madeleine Grunde-McLaughlin, Sarah Cen, Jevan Hutson, Jamie Morgenstern, Tadayoshi Kohno

item.title: Lasso: Towards Sustainable AI-Generated Media Detection with Intel QAT On-Chip Compression
item.description: Synthetic text, images, and video are rising. Software-only detectors are power-hungry, too slow, and costly, and do not scale with demand. When software cannot scale, historically hardware often comes to the rescue. We perform the first reverse engineering of a compression accelerator--Intel QuickAssist Technology (QAT) microarchitecture and--find different amount of time on each, a novel data structure-dependent property. Using this information, we then build Lasso, a low-cost, high-performance detector for AI-generated content that turns the accelerator into a measuring instrument. For text detection, Lasso achieves 100% accuracy on original DetectRL text and retains 92% average accuracy after paraphrasing, compared with 78% for Binoculars and 55% for DetectGPT. Across original, paraphrased, and perturbed text, it achieves 82% average accuracy, outperforming all five baselines. With topic, length, and formatting matched, accuracy reaches 95% for instruction-tuned generators, including when the tested generator is unseen. On RAID, accuracy averages 82% when trained on one generator and tested on another, and 74% across eight held-out domains. Detection takes 0.74 microseconds, a speedup of at least 83,784x across five baselines. At the same time, Lasso consumes over 99% less energy per document than both Binoculars and DetectGPT. At the same time, Lasso detects AI-generated videos, software code, and images with 67.5%, 70% and 78% accuracy, respectively, with low latency and power opening avenues for practical real time and edge device detection of multimodality AI artifacts for the first time. No other compared technique supports detection across all four modalities: text, video, images, and code.
item.dc:creator: Darsh Asher, Joshua Kalyanapu, Kaushal Mhapsekar, Bita Aslrousta, Amna Hassan, Debayan Sengupta, Samira Mirbagher Ajorpaz

item.title: Benchmark Factory: Agentic Benchmark Creation via Dataset Curation and Label-Free Quality Anchors
item.description: Teams deploying coding agents need benchmarks built from their own code, but curating and validating them by hand is resource intensive, and an unvalidated benchmark can mislead silently. We present Benchmark Factory, an autonomous meta-agent loop with human checkpoints: an LLM agent writes sourcing queries over landed production code changes, runs models of known relative strength on each candidate, diagnoses why a candidate fails, and repairs it by editing its queries, prompts, and configuration until it clears quality anchors that need no per-task human labels. We used Benchmark Factory to build benchmarks for five developer cohorts at our organization. Engineering raters scored a 5% sample 2.3 for task quality and 2.6 for grader verdicts on a 1-to-3 scale. On configurations never used to build them, the benchmarks ranked Claude Opus~4.7 at high reasoning effort above low effort (60.6% vs. 54.4% of tasks passed, $p=0.002$) and GPT-5.5 above GPT-5.4 (65.8% vs. 60.5%, $p=0.004$); 9 of the 10 per-cohort comparisons pointed the same way. A deliberately trivial benchmark failed the anchors; five broken graders failed them, even under a relaxed rule fixed in advance that the real grader passes; and with model labels shuffled so that no true ordering existed, random redraws of a candidate passed in at most 1.4% of simulations. The anchors are necessary, not sufficient, conditions for a valid benchmark, designed to focus human review on what the loop cannot repair.
item.dc:creator: Shervin Shahidi, James Poon, Hang Xie, Kenneth O. Xu, Robin H{\aa}kanson, Vikram Nair, Jens Pillgram-Larsen, Nachiappan Nagappan

item.title: Self-Improvement Memory Enables Continual Recursive Self-Improvement
item.description: Harness optimization is often studied with a fixed policy model and benchmark. When either changes, the optimizer must decide which parts of an evolved harness to reuse or revise, but the harness alone may not explain why earlier edits were made or how they performed. In this work, we study Continual Recursive Self-Improvement (CRSI), a setting for continuing existing harness-optimization methods across compatible benchmarks or policy models. We propose Self-Improvement Memory (SIM) for the harness optimizer, rather than the task-solving policy. SIM groups edits by recurring harness problem and records their rationale, predicted and observed outcomes, and evaluation context. New attempts extend this history as optimization continues. In our experiments across four domains, SIM achieves higher final scores than harness-only and root-cause-only continuation in cross-dataset and pairwise cross-model comparisons. Across ten independent source runs in coding, paired continuations with SIM improve final scores by an average of 2.36 points over harness-only continuation ($p=0.003$).
item.dc:creator: Xin Yu, Fei Xia, Jiaqi Pan, Youbao Tang, Chengzhi Liu, Adams Yu, Sicong Jiang, Yanfei Chen, Lingzhou Xue, Ting Yu

item.title: KUDEX: A Zero-Shot Decompositional Framework for Logical Analysis in Natural Language
item.description: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at generating fluent text, they often struggle with multi-step logical reasoning with inferential connections among statements. We introduce KUDEX (Knowledge-Upward-Downward Reasoning Extension), a novel zero-shot, decompositional framework for analyzing and verifying logical relationships in natural language. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on surface-level entailment checks, KUDEX leverages LLMs to decompose reasoning into atomic primitives and constructs transparent reasoning graphs that serve both as execution traces and audit logs. Our framework includes a general prompt adaptation pipeline that adapts to diverse reasoning tasks without additional fine-tuning or domain-specific pipelines. Through comprehensive experiments on benchmarks across four domains, we demonstrate that KUDEX provides superior performance compared to existing methods, offering a more granular and robust framework for assessing logical relationships between statements.
item.dc:creator: Zixu Zhao, Tianhang Zhang, Tong He, Zheng Zhang

item.title: Rethinking Offline On-Policy Distillation: From Scalar Advantages to Distributional Supervision
item.description: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher capabilities through token-level feedback on student-generated trajectories, but repeatedly evaluating fresh rollouts with the teacher is computationally expensive. Offline methods such as Lightning OPD reduce this cost by caching recorded tokens' teacher log-probabilities on fixed reference rollouts. By extending the idea to a multi-turn agentic search setup, we find that it consistently underperforms the SFT starting point trained by the same teacher. We empirically observe greater teacher--reference mismatch than in mathematical reasoning and post-training distributional flattening, and theoretically show that scalar advantage supervision on fixed rollouts admits solutions with flattened output distributions under suitable conditions. Motivated by these findings, we propose Distributional On-Policy Distillation (DistOPD), a simple yet effective offline OPD method that retains candidate-token probabilities from both reference and teacher at selected positions and aggregates the remaining parts into a residual token. On agentic search, DistOPD achieves performance comparable to online OPD while improving student--teacher alignment and using training GPU-hours comparable to Lightning OPD.
item.dc:creator: Qi Sun, Siyue Zhang, Tingyu Song, Yilun Zhao, Chen Zhao

item.title: RSIMed: Scaling Medical Foundation Models beyond Limited Clinical Data via Retrieval-Grounded Self-Evolution
item.description: Rare diseases are hard to diagnose, and the labeled clinical records needed to train models for them are few, private, and slow to extend, since a specialist must read every case. A model that writes its own training tasks could learn beyond these records, but no program can check a model-written diagnosis, and a wrong answer key corrupts training. To tackle this dilemma between data scarcity and difficulty of data annotations, we introduce RSIMed, Recursive Self-Improvement in Medicine, one of the first self-evolving pipelines in which a task proposer co-evolves in context with a diagnostic solver on real clinical records. Seeded by training admissions, a frozen copy of the solver writes each clinical question from retrieved medical evidence, so its answer rests on a source, and steers topics and difficulty toward what the solver still gets wrong. On rare-disease diagnosis from MIMIC-IV admissions, the accuracy of RSIMed-27B grows linearly with training compute, while a static pool of generated tasks collapses. Without any external model, RSIMed-27B and RSIMed-9B reach 0.516 and 0.488 diagnostic accuracy, above every off-the-shelf GPT-5.6 setting, whose best reaches 0.399 at 38 times the inference cost of RSIMed-27B. Tasks written by four external teachers, including GPT-5.5, train a less accurate diagnostician than the solver's own. Trained only on diagnosis, RSIMed-RL-27B also improves on the physician-written tasks of HealthBench Professional, from 0.291 to 0.303 in adjusted score.
